periods.public: The panel discusses which historical records will best reveal the risks of the new system. They focus on financial patterns, operational stability, and human resource constraints.

lines.Midori: Suggests looking into ownership of past failures and rule changes.
lines.Ryuji: Emphasizes the need to check depot calendars and yard hardware.
lines.May: Proposes checking the dispatch tool history and the 2018 data move.
lines.Misaki: Focuses on administrator retirements and supervisor reactions to rollouts.
lines.Benjamin: Suggests reviewing board minutes and renewal invoices.

lines.Midori: Agrees with the need for operational data.
lines.Ryuji: Asks if others agree on the priority of the depot floor.
lines.May: Comments on the danger of outdated tools.
lines.Misaki: Notes the risk of losing institutional knowledge.
lines.Benjamin: Points out that budget structures often hide true costs.

periods.public: Participants share the implications of their findings without naming vendors. They debate the trade-offs between fixed configurations, external partners, and internal hosting.

lines.Midori: Shares that past outages were unowned and rules changed quickly.
lines.Ryuji: Reports that peak seasons are brutal and yard gear is old.
lines.May: Mentions that internal tools were neglected and external data moves failed.
lines.Misaki: Highlights the lack of available admins and supervisor resistance.
lines.Benjamin: Reveals that operating costs creep up while capital is cut.

lines.Midori: Asks how to avoid the 'no one in charge' scenario.
lines.Ryuji: Questions if any plan can actually survive the November peak.
lines.May: Warns against relying on outside firms for data.
lines.Misaki: Asks who will actually train the staff if admins are gone.
lines.Benjamin: Warns against fragmented licensing that increases costs.

lines.Midori: Suggests a need for a single point of accountability.
lines.Ryuji: Argues for a solution that respects the physical reality of the yard.
lines.May: Argues for a system that doesn't age out quickly.
lines.Misaki: Emphasizes the need for on-site presence during rollout.
lines.Benjamin: Suggests a predictable cost model is essential.

periods.public: The panel evaluates the four candidates against the discovered risks. They weigh the benefits of on-site engineering versus hosted flexibility and fixed pricing.

lines.Midori: Prefers the fixed configuration and regional team for accountability.
lines.Ryuji: Prefers the on-site engineering and local server approach.
lines.May: Likes the hosted suite for avoiding the 'aging in place' problem.
lines.Misaki: Favors the on-site presence to help the stretched staff.
lines.Benjamin: Favors the fixed configuration to avoid cost creep.

lines.Midori: Questions if the on-site approach is too risky for the budget.
lines.Ryuji: Questions if a hosted system can handle the yard's reality.
lines.May: Objects to the complexity of modular licensing.
lines.Misaki: Argues that without on-site help, the rollout will fail.
lines.Benjamin: Points out that a subscription with a partner might hide costs.

lines.Midori: Leans toward the regional team for balance.
lines.Ryuji: Sticks to the need for physical presence.
lines.May: Agrees with the regional team approach.
lines.Misaki: Sticks to the on-site engineering preference.
lines.Benjamin: Argues for the most predictable financial path.

seats.Benjamin: Cares about long-term hidden costs. He argues for financial predictability and avoids fragmented billing.
seats.Midori: Cares about accountability and adaptability. She seeks a balance between a clear owner and a flexible plan.
seats.May: Cares about technical longevity and the quality of implementation. She dislikes systems that decay or are poorly migrated.
seats.Ryuji: Cares about the physical operational environment. He prioritizes solutions that work with old hardware and tight schedules.
seats.Misaki: Cares about the burden on personnel. She prioritizes ease of transition and direct assistance for the staff.
